title: Many rites (CCC 1200–1206)
hook: Latin, Byzantine, Alexandrian, Syriac, Armenian, Maronite, Chaldean: one faith, many forms

segments.voice: Yesterday, the church building, and the ambo, where the word of God is proclaimed. Your line was each place speaks.

Two Catholic churches, one Sunday morning, a few streets apart. In the first, the priest stands at a plain altar facing the people, and an organ plays. In the second, painted icons stretch across the front, incense hangs in the air, and nearly everything is sung, back and forth between priest and people. The prayers are different. The vestments are different. Even the name is different: in the second church people may call it the Divine Liturgy. Yet both are Catholic, both are in communion with the Pope, and both celebrate the same Eucharist. How?
screen: `TWO CHURCHES, ONE SUNDAY.` → `ORGAN HERE, ICONS AND INCENSE THERE.` → `BOTH CATHOLIC.`

segments.voice: Day nine hundred forty-three met one Eastern Catholic church; today, the bigger picture. The word is rite. In ordinary speech a rite is a ceremony. In the Catechism it means something bigger: a whole family of worship, with its own prayers, music, calendar and ways, handed down in one part of the Church. The Catechism starts with what doesn't change: the one mystery of Christ, his death and resurrection, celebrated everywhere. Then a striking claim: that mystery is so rich that no single liturgical tradition can say all of it. As the Gospel traveled, it took root among different peoples, and their worship grew in harmony with their languages and cultures. The Catechism names the traditions in use today. The Latin, mainly the Roman rite, along with some local and religious-order rites. The Byzantine. The Alexandrian, or Coptic. The Syriac. The Armenian. The Maronite. The Chaldean. Repeating the Second Vatican Council, it says the Church holds all lawfully recognized rites to be of equal right and dignity, and wants to keep them alive and growing. Not a main rite and some exotic extras. Equal. But there's a limit: diversity mustn't damage unity. The rites stay one by keeping the same apostolic faith, the same sacraments, and communion with the bishops and the Pope. So the icons and the organ aren't rivals. They're two ways of saying one thing, each fully at home in the one Church.
screen: `A RITE: A WHOLE FAMILY OF WORSHIP.` · `ONE MYSTERY, TOO RICH FOR ONE FORM.` · `EQUAL RIGHT AND DIGNITY.` · `DIVERSITY MUST NOT HARM UNITY.`

segments.voice: Let the names go by slowly, one for each breath: Latin, Byzantine, Alexandrian, Syriac, Armenian, Maronite, Chaldean. Notice which one you know least about, and just hold that name. If you pray, hold up the Catholics of that rite, wherever they are.
Rite. Not one ceremony but a whole tradition of worship, with its own prayers and ways, celebrating the one mystery of Christ. Today's word.
Your line: one faith, many forms. Equal right, equal dignity. Rest well.

howItsDone: Roman-rite parishes celebrate the Mass, while Byzantine Catholic parishes celebrate what they call the Divine Liturgy; each Eastern Catholic church keeps its own liturgy, calendar and customs.

chat.says: I went to a Catholic church with icons and chanting. Was that even a real Catholic Mass?
options: Yes. It's another rite, a whole family of worship, equal in dignity with all the others.
No; a church with icons and chanting must have broken away from Rome long ago.
Probably not; anything without an organ and a plain altar isn't Catholic.
chat.meaning: The Catechism names many rites, Latin, Byzantine, Coptic and more, of equal right and dignity, one in faith, sacraments and communion with the Pope.
